title: Setting Up Your First Bird Cage
excerpt: Everything you need to know about choosing the right cage, placement, and essential accessories for your new feathered friend.
content:
Choosing the right cage is one of the most important decisions you'll make as a bird owner. The cage should be large enough for your bird to spread its wings fully and move comfortably.

## Size Matters

As a general rule, the cage should be at least 1.5 times the wingspan of your bird in width and depth. For active species like budgerigars and cockatiels, bigger is always better.

## Placement

Place the cage in a social area where your bird can observe family activity, but away from direct sunlight, drafts, and kitchen fumes. Birds are sensitive to Teflon fumes and strong cooking odors.

## Essential Accessories

- Multiple perches of varying diameters
- Food and water dishes (stainless steel preferred)
- Cuttlebone for calcium
- A variety of safe toys for mental stimulation
- Cage liner or paper for easy cleaning

## Safety First

Avoid cages with zinc or lead components. Ensure bar spacing is appropriate for your bird species to prevent escape or injury.
author: The Aviary Guide Team

title: Understanding Bird Body Language
excerpt: Learn to read your bird's signals — from crest position to tail fanning — and build a stronger bond through communication.
content:
Birds communicate extensively through body language. Learning to read these signals helps you understand your bird's mood and needs.

## Crest Position (Cockatiels & Cockatoos)

- Raised crest: Alert, curious, or excited
- Flat crest: Relaxed or content
- Crest held back: Fearful or defensive

## Feather Language

- Fluffed feathers: Content, warm, or possibly ill
- Sleek feathers: Alert and comfortable
- Rapid tail fanning: Excitement or agitation

## Vocal Cues

Different species have unique vocalizations. Budgerigars chatter when happy, while doves coo softly when content. Learning your species' normal sounds helps you detect distress early.

## Building Trust

Move slowly around new birds. Offer treats from your hand and allow them to approach on their terms. Consistency and patience are key.
author: The Aviary Guide Team

title: Seasonal Diet Changes for Pet Birds
excerpt: How to adjust your bird's nutrition throughout the year for optimal health and vitality.
content:
Just as wild birds adapt their diet to seasonal availability, pet birds benefit from dietary variety throughout the year.

## Spring & Breeding Season

Increase protein with egg food or sprouted seeds. Provide extra calcium through cuttlebone and mineral blocks. Fresh greens become especially important.

## Summer

Offer hydrating foods like cucumber, melon, and leafy greens. Ensure fresh water is changed frequently. Avoid leaving fresh food in the cage for extended periods in warm weather.

## Autumn

Gradually increase seed content as birds naturally prepare for cooler months. Introduce seasonal fruits like apples and berries.

## Winter

Maintain consistent feeding schedules. Warm, cooked grains like rice and quinoa can be offered as occasional treats. Monitor weight as activity levels may decrease.

title: Creating a Bird-Safe Home Environment
excerpt: Common household hazards every bird owner should know about — and how to bird-proof your living space.
content:
Birds are curious and fragile creatures. Many common household items pose serious risks.

## Toxic Substances

- Avocado, chocolate, caffeine, and alcohol are toxic to all birds
- Non-stick cookware releases fumes lethal to birds when overheated
- Many houseplants are toxic — research before placing plants near cages

## Physical Hazards

- Open windows and doors without screens
- Ceiling fans
- Open water containers (toilets, sinks)
- Electrical cords
- Small spaces where birds can become trapped

## Safe Exploration

When allowing out-of-cage time, designate a bird-safe room. Remove hazards, cover mirrors, and ensure all windows are closed or screened. Supervise at all times.
